# Ukraine’s Exposure Grows as Satellite Use Is Restricted and Russia Escalates

A huge attack cut power to 600,000 people in Kyiv, and a Pentagon-funded satellite internet program appeared to be curbed without warning.

[Audio 2](https://static.nytimes.com/narrated-articles/synthetic/article-71e17d98-10c1-5731-98e6-fe9585bad814/job-1792010885639/article-71e17d98-10c1-5731-98e6-fe9585bad814-job-1792010885639.mp3)

![Image 1: A woman kneeling on the ground and using a cellphone, wearing a dressing gown and with a bleeding, bandaged face.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/14/multimedia/14int-ukraine-vulnerability-01-qbck/14int-ukraine-vulnerability-01-qbck-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

A wounded woman at the site of a strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Tuesday.Credit...Yan Dobronosov/Reuters

[![Image 2: Constant Méheut](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2022/04/04/reader-center/author-constant-meheut/author-constant-meheut-thumbLarge.png)](https://www.nytimes.com/by/constant-meheut)

By [Constant Méheut](https://www.nytimes.com/by/constant-meheut)

Reporting from Kyiv, Ukraine

Oct. 14, 2026 Updated 4:47 p.m. ET

[Leer en español](https://www.nytimes.com/es/2026/10/14/espanol/mundo/ucrania-guerra-rusia-ataques-trump.html "Read in Spanish")

[See more of our coverage in your search results.Encuentra más de nuestra cobertura en los resultados de búsqueda.Add The New York Times on Google Agrega The New York Times en Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?cs=0&hl=en&q=nytimes.com)

Nearly five years into its fight for national survival, Ukraine has entered a moment of intense vulnerability, under growing pressure not only from Russia but also now from the United States.

A double blow came overnight on Wednesday.

Ukraine said that its military, with no warning, had lost some critical access to a military version of Starlink, a pillar of its battlefield communications. Kyiv relies on the satellite internet network, known as Starshield, which is paid for by the Pentagon. That led Ukrainian officials and analysts to surmise that the restrictions had come from Washington, as President Trump is [locked in his latest feud](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/11/world/europe/trump-zelensky-diesel-energy-russia-.html) with Ukraine’s leadership.

At the same time, Russia unleashed dozens of ballistic missiles in a broad attack on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure early Wednesday, cutting power to 600,000 people in the capital, Kyiv. It was a dark omen for a rapidly approaching winter in which Russia is gearing up to try to push Ukraine to the breaking point as Kyiv runs low on lifesaving air defenses.

It was unclear how long the Starshield restrictions would remain in place. Still, the Trump administration’s treatment of Ukraine has caused outrage in a country already reeling from a string of challenges.

Its [energy system is at risk of collapse](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/world/europe/russia-ukraine-winter.html) in the coming months as Russia pounds power plants and substations, trying to deprive Ukrainians of heat and water. Its [economy is being pushed to the brink](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/world/europe/russia-diesel-trump.html) by Russian strikes on its ports, warehouses and steel factories. And its budget faces a multibillion-dollar gap this year and next that could leave its military severely underfunded.

Title: Is Universal Basic Income the Answer to A.I.-Fueled Job Losses?

[Video 3](https://vp.nyt.com/video/2026/10/08/180477_1_08visualUploader-3618_wg_1080p.mp4)

## What a Year of Free Money Meant: Softer Diapers, Clean Laundry, a Visit to Six Flags

For more than a year, The New York Times followed recipients of universal basic income programs, which Elon Musk and other tech leaders have promoted as a solution to A.I.-fueled job losses.

## What a Year of Free Money Meant: Softer Diapers, Clean Laundry, a Visit to Six Flags

For more than a year, The New York Times followed recipients of universal basic income programs, which Elon Musk and other tech leaders have promoted as a solution to A.I.-fueled job losses.

Credit...

Listen

· 18:36 min

By [Eli Tan](https://www.nytimes.com/by/eli-tan) and Rachel Bujalski

Photographs by Rachel Bujalski

Eli Tan and Rachel Bujalski followed families on guaranteed income programs around the San Francisco Bay Area.

Oct. 12, 2026

One morning in December 2024, Mikole Weeks, then 35, received a phone call with surprising news. She had been chosen for an experimental program called guaranteed basic income, and it came with cash: $1,330 a month for an entire year, with no strings attached for how it could be spent.

“It felt like another chance to turn my life around,” said Ms. Weeks, a single mother and a part-time house cleaner in Santa Cruz, Calif.

Only it did not turn out to be quite that simple.

For decades, people have [debated the merits](https://www.nytimes.com/2016/06/01/business/economy/universal-basic-income-poverty.html) of guaranteed income programs, also called universal basic income, as an alternative or complement to traditional welfare. Driving the efforts is the idea that the most effective way to improve people’s lives is to give them cash and let them spend it how they want.

The concept resurged in popularity a decade ago, driven by fears of automation and rising wealth inequality. Proponents argued that permanent payments would raise the standard of living for those on the margins, and ultimately lift millions off welfare. Critics contended that giving people money unconditionally would deter them from working in the first place.

In the age of artificial intelligence, these programs have again become [a hot topic](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/22/business/dealbook/newsom-universal-basic-capital-ai.html). Tech titans including Elon Musk, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic have hailed basic income as a solution to [A.I.-fueled job losses](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/19/technology/meta-layoffs-ai.html). In April, Mr. Musk posted that “universal HIGH INCOME” was the best way to deal with unemployment caused by the powerful technology. In June, Dr. Amodei suggested a tax on A.I. companies as one way to fund these payments.

Across Silicon Valley, experimental guaranteed income programs have quietly taken off. Google began funding six different initiatives in 2022 as part of a [$50 million donation](https://realestate.withgoogle.com/bay-housing/#:~:text=to%20end%20homelessness-,In%20addition,-to%20Google%20land) to nonprofits in the San Francisco Bay Area, saying basic income could be a novel way to prevent homelessness in one of the nation’s most expensive locations. Each program has hundreds of participants who receive around $1,000 a month, and academics study the results. State and federal tax laws limit the lengths of the programs and the payment amounts.
